content: Horseradish, scientifically known as Armoracia rusticana (synonym Cochlearia armoracia), is a perennial plant belonging to the Brassicaceae family, which also includes mustard, wasabi, and cabbages. It is believed to have originated in southeastern Europe and western Asia, but it is now cultivated and consumed globally. The plant can grow up to 1.5 meters (approximately five feet) in height and is primarily cultivated for its large, white, tapered root. The root itself has little to no aroma in its intact state. However, when it is cut or grated, enzymes released from the damaged plant cells break down a glucosinolate compound called sinigrin, resulting in the production of allyl isothiocyanate, also known as mustard oil. This compound is responsible for the characteristic pungency of horseradish, which can irritate the sinuses and eyes. If the grated root is not used immediately or preserved in vinegar, it darkens, loses its pungency, and develops an unpleasantly bitter taste when exposed to air and heat. Historical Context Horseradish has been cultivated since ancient times. In Greek mythology, the Delphic Oracle reportedly told Apollo that horseradish was as valuable as its weight in gold. The plant was known in Egypt as early as 1500 BCE and has been traditionally used by Eastern European Jews during Passover Seders. Roman agricultural texts, such as those by Cato, mention horseradish, and a mural in Pompeii depicts the plant. Pliny the Elder, in his Natural History, likely referred to horseradish under the name Amoracia, recommending it for its medicinal properties. The Greeks may have identified it as raphanos agrios or wild radish. During the Middle Ages, both the root and leaves of horseradish were used medicinally, while the root also became a popular condiment for meats in Germany, Scandinavia, and Britain. The plant was introduced to North America during the Colonial period. William Turner referred to horseradish as Red Cole in his Herbal (1551–1568), though not as a condiment. John Gerard, in his Generall Historie of Plantes (1597), described it as raphanus rusticanus, noting its wild occurrence in parts of England and its use in German cuisine as a sauce for fish when mixed with vinegar. Cultivation Practices Horseradish is a hardy perennial that thrives in USDA hardiness zones 2 through 9. It can also be grown as an annual in other zones, though it performs best in regions with a long growing season and sufficiently cold winters to induce dormancy. After the first frost in autumn kills the leaves, the root is harvested and divided. If left undisturbed, horseradish can spread aggressively through underground shoots, potentially becoming invasive. Older roots that remain in the ground become woody and are no longer suitable for culinary use, though they can still be divided to propagate new plants. Pests and Diseases Horseradish is susceptible to damage from imported cabbageworms (Artogeia rapae), a common caterpillar pest. The adult form of this pest is a white butterfly with black spots on its forewings, often seen flying around plants during the day. The caterpillars are velvety green with faint yellow stripes running lengthwise along their backs and sides. They overwinter in green pupal cases, and adult butterflies emerge after the last frost, remaining active throughout the growing season. There are typically 3 to 5 overlapping generations per year. The caterpillars feed on horseradish leaves, creating large, ragged holes while leaving the main veins intact. Handpicking is an effective method of controlling this pest. Commercial Production Collinsville, Illinois, is known as the Horseradish Capital of the World and hosts an annual International Horseradish Festival each June. The region produces approximately 60% of the world's commercially grown horseradish, with 85% of production concentrated in Southwestern Illinois. Other significant horseradish-growing regions in the United States include Wisconsin and Northern California. Culinary Applications The grated root of the horseradish plant, often mixed with vinegar, is referred to as prepared horseradish. This preparation is white to creamy beige in color and can be refrigerated for several months, though it will eventually darken and lose its flavor, signaling the need for replacement. The leaves of the plant, known as horseradish greens, are edible but not commonly consumed. While horseradish is technically a root, it is primarily used as a condiment or ingredient. In the United States, prepared horseradish is a common component of Bloody Mary cocktails, cocktail sauces, and spreads for meats, poultry, fish, and sandwiches. The fast-food chain Arby’s incorporates horseradish into its Horsey Sauce, a condiment offered alongside ketchup, mustard, and mayonnaise. Gold's Horseradish, based in New York, is the largest U.S. manufacturer of prepared horseradish, producing approximately 2.5 million jars annually. In the United Kingdom, horseradish sauce, made from grated horseradish root and cream, is a popular accompaniment to roast beef and other dishes. Tewkesbury mustard, a blend of mustard and grated horseradish, originated in medieval England and was even mentioned by Shakespeare. In Eastern European Jewish cuisine, a sweetened horseradish-vinegar sauce called chrain traditionally accompanies gefilte fish. There are two varieties of chrain: red (mixed with beetroot) and white (without beetroot). Similar preparations are popular in Poland (chrzan), Hungary (torma), Romania (hrean), and Bulgaria (хрян). Horseradish is a traditional Easter dish in many Eastern and Central European countries, often mixed with cream, hard-boiled eggs, or apples. In Slovenia and the Italian region of Friuli Venezia Giulia, horseradish is a staple of Easter meals. In Poland's Silesia region, horseradish soup is a traditional Easter Sunday dish. Additionally, horseradish is often dyed green and used as a substitute for the more expensive wasabi in sushi, even in Japan, where it is referred to as Western wasabi. Nutritional Composition Horseradish is a source of essential minerals, including potassium, calcium, magnesium, and phosphorus. It also contains volatile oils, such as mustard oil, which exhibit antibiotic properties. Fresh horseradish provides an average of 79.31 mg of vitamin C per 100 grams of raw root. Research Applications The enzyme horseradish peroxidase (HRP), derived from the plant, is widely used in molecular biology, particularly for antibody detection. It plays a critical role in immunohistochemistry (IHC), a branch of pathology that involves staining tissue biopsies to identify specific biomarkers, often for cancer diagnosis. HRP is conjugated to polymers along with immunoglobulins that bind to primary antibodies targeting specific cellular markers. The enzyme catalyzes the conversion of 3,3-diaminobenzidine (DAB) into a yellowish-brown insoluble compound, which is visible under a microscope and aids pathologists in diagnosing cancer. HRP is also used in diagnostic materials for detecting glucose in blood or urine. Medicinal Uses Horseradish roots are known for their diuretic properties and have been used to treat minor health conditions such as urinary tract infections, bronchitis, sinus congestion, and coughs. Certain compounds in horseradish have demonstrated antibacterial activity, effectively killing some bacterial strains.
